cards.title: Verify AI crawler access with robots.txt and rendering tests
cards.summary: Check that GPTBot, PerplexityBot and Google AI Overview bots can access your store pages before doing anything else for AI visibility.
cards.use_when: Baseline technical audit of an ecommerce site before investing in AEO/GEO content or PR, or when AI engines never cite your product or category pages.
steps: Understand that AI search engines send crawler bots to your site to learn what you sell; if those bots are blocked, the store is invisible in AI answers regardless of content quality.
Run a free AI bot access checker against your domain to test GPTBot (ChatGPT), PerplexityBot, and the Google AI Overview search bot, and confirm each returns a pass.

Open your robots.txt file and confirm it does not disallow AI crawlers; most legacy robots.txt files were written only with Googlebot in mind. The presenter says to ask in the comments for a fix guide, so treat remediation as a technical task for your developer.

Test whether key page content (title, meta description, headings, body copy) renders without JavaScript, since many AI bots do not execute JavaScript; use a free render-comparison tool to see what text appears with JS disabled.
If product names, specs, pricing or category copy only appear after JS execution, work with your developer to server-render or pre-render those elements.
Re-test after any site change, since theme updates and app installs on platforms like Shopify can silently reintroduce blocking.
caveats: The presenter notes the fix for JS-heavy sites is technical and offers a guide rather than a universal solution in the video; results of the validation tools should be verified against the current tool interface.
Tool links referenced in the video are not specified here; use any bot-access checker and JS-render checker and verify they cover current AI crawler user agents.

cards.title: Submit sitemaps and confirm indexation as an AI visibility prerequisite
cards.summary: AI engines pull fresh information from Google and Bing, so an unindexed store will not be recommended in AI answers.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ecommerce store for AI visibility, or diagnosing why AI engines describe your brand inaccurately or not at all.
steps: Recognize the dependency: AI search engines like ChatGPT lean on traditional search engines (the presenter notes Microsoft owns roughly 50% of ChatGPT and that Bing feeds it), so pages missing from Bing or Google are effectively missing from AI answers.
In Google Search Console, go to Indexing > Sitemaps, enter your sitemap URL (typically yoursite.com/sitemap.xml), and submit; the presenter's example picked up 94 pages with a successful status.
Repeat the same sitemap submission in Bing Webmaster Tools, which matters disproportionately for ChatGPT-sourced answers.
Spot-check indexation by typing site:yourdomain.com into Google search to see which of your product, category and content pages are actually indexed.
Re-submit or investigate whenever new product or collection pages are not appearing, since unindexed SKU pages cannot be surfaced to AI shoppers.
caveats: Sitemap submission does not guarantee indexation; crawl budget, page quality and technical issues still apply.
Verify the current navigation paths in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, as interfaces change.

cards.title: Publish an About/Facts page as structured brand context for AI
cards.summary: A facts page giving what you do, your USPs and how long you've operated gives AI engines the raw material to describe and recommend you correctly.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing the homepage/about section of an ecommerce store so AI engines can state accurate brand facts in recommendations.
steps: Add an About Us or Facts page to your store if one does not exist; many stores skip this, leaving AI with no authoritative brand description.
List what you sell, your key differentiators/USPs, how long the business has existed, and any relevant credentials in plain, factual language.
Keep the facts consistent with what appears in directories, review platforms and schema so AI does not encounter conflicting claims.
Update the page as the business changes (new categories, certifications, milestones) so AI recommendations stay current.
Treat this page as the canonical fact source you will later point schema and directory listings toward.
caveats: The presenter's claim that adding a facts page will make visibility 'grow' is a directional expectation, not a measured benchmark.
Facts pages do not substitute for product-level crawlability and content quality.

cards.title: Implement schema markup so AI bots parse your store without guessing
cards.summary: Structured data spells out your business, products and social profiles in a machine-readable format AI crawlers read reliably.
cards.use_when: Adding or auditing structured data on an ecommerce site to improve how LLMs interpret brand and product information.
steps: Understand structured data as a code snippet AI crawlers read easily; without it, AI engines may guess or omit details about your brand.
Add Organization schema to the homepage including founding date, description, and links to social profiles; this signals that you are a proper, reputable business.
Use a schema generator tool to select a schema type, fill in the relevant fields, and copy the generated code onto the appropriate page.
Apply the other schema types recommended in the source checklist to their matching page types (e.g. product-related types on product pages) rather than dumping all schema on one template.
Link your YouTube channel and social profiles from your website and include them in schema markup alongside the rest of your brand data.
Validate the markup after deployment so errors do not silently defeat the purpose.
caveats: Schema improves interpretability but does not guarantee recommendation; the presenter treats it as one of several inputs.
Exact schema types beyond Organization are in the linked checklist, not enumerated in the video.

cards.title: Front-load answers on product and category pages with a TL;DR
cards.summary: Put a direct 2-4 sentence answer and a TL;DR at the top of every important page because most AI citations come from the first third of the page.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting product pages, category pages, buying guides and landing pages so AI extracts your content as the cited answer.
steps: Open each key page with a direct 2-4 sentence answer to the core question the shopper or AI is asking, rather than a slow marketing build-up.
Follow it with a TL;DR summary block, so both users and AI crawlers get the essential value immediately.
The presenter cites that over 44% of AI citations come from the first third of the page, so move key facts (materials, sizing, use cases, who it's for) above the fold and above decorative sections.
Write in natural language rather than keyword-stuffed phrasing, since AI engines parse natural-language queries and prefer natural-language answers.
Apply the same structure to comparison and informational pages, not just product pages.
Keep updating the top sections as facts change so the first third of the page is always the most accurate.
caveats: The 44% first-third citation figure is the presenter's cited statistic; treat it as a directional heuristic rather than a fixed rule for your site.
Front-loading answers does not excuse poor product information further down the page — shoppers still read details.

cards.title: Build FAQ sections from 'People Also Ask' to grow topical authority
cards.summary: Harvest the questions Google surfaces for your topic and answer them at the bottom of every important page to demonstrate expertise to AI.
cards.use_when: Adding Q&A coverage to product pages, category pages or buying guides to increase the chance AI engines treat your store as the expert source.
steps: Search your topic (e.g. 'self storage software') in Google and scroll to the 'People Also Asked' section.
Copy those exact questions — Google is literally telling you what people ask about the topic — and draft clear answers.
Add the questions and answers as an FAQ section at the bottom of every important page on the site.
The presenter's stated purpose is boosting topical authority: showing AI engines you are an expert, which in turn lifts visibility.
Repeat per page type so category pages, product pages and guides each answer their own cluster of questions.
Refresh FAQs periodically so answers reflect current pricing, specs and policies.
caveats: The link between FAQ sections and AI recommendation is the presenter's asserted mechanism, not a measured guarantee.
Avoid dumping irrelevant questions; mismatched FAQs can hurt user experience on purchase pages.

cards.title: Use comparison tables and head-to-head competitor pages to win AI recommendations
cards.summary: Head-to-head comparison pages and tables give AI engines an easy, digestible reason to recommend you over larger competitors it already knows.
cards.use_when: Competing against bigger, better-known brands in your category in AI search, or structuring comparison content on an ecommerce site.
steps: Pick three to four larger competitors than you and write head-to-head pages comparing you versus competitor A, B, C and D.
Break down pros and cons of each option honestly so the page is credible, while clearly explaining why your product is better for the relevant buyer.
The presenter's logic: AI engines already know the big players, so comparing yourself to them supplies the reasoning AI needs to recommend you above them.
For any head-to-head or comparison content, include a comparison table near the top; tables are an easy-to-digest structure for AI engines to lift into answers.
Extend the same approach to comparison tables on your own category and product pages where buyers evaluate alternatives.
Keep the comparison facts accurate — pricing, features, specs — since inaccurate claims undermine credibility with both buyers and AI.
caveats: The presenter frames this as particularly effective for smaller businesses competing with much bigger players; it is not a guarantee of outranking the larger brand.
Legality and platform rules around comparative advertising vary by market; get claims checked where required.

cards.title: Replace vague claims with hard numbers, expert quotes and original data
cards.summary: High-quality content with specific figures, named expert quotes and at least one piece of original data is more likely to be cited by AI engines.
cards.use_when: Improving the citability of product pages, buying guides, blog posts and category content that currently relies on generic marketing language.
steps: Audit content for vague claims such as 'many users prefer' and replace them with hard numbers and percentages wherever you have evidence (e.g. real customer results, review counts, test findings).
Add direct quotes from named team members who have a credible public presence, such as a strong LinkedIn profile; the presenter says this boosts visibility.

Include at least one piece of original data per important page — a survey, internal benchmark or industry finding AI cannot get elsewhere — since AI engines look for unique data to make answers more credible.
Consider producing an industry report or data roundup with original sourcing to position your brand as the category leader and give AI a citable primary source.
Apply the same rigor to glossary pages and statistics roundups, which the presenter identifies as content types that get cited.
Only publish data and quotes that are real and verifiable; fabricated figures are a reputational and legal risk.
caveats: The presenter asserts high-quality, original data creates a 'massive advantage'; this is expert opinion, not a measured effect size.
Small stores may have limited original data; customer outcome metrics or aggregated review data can serve as a starting point, but must be honest.

cards.title: Refresh evergreen content and surface a clear last-updated date
cards.summary: Stale content loses to fresh competitors in AI answers, so revisit key pages every couple of months and show the last-updated date.
cards.use_when: Maintaining a content library or buying-guide set on an ecommerce site that has not been refreshed recently and is losing AI citations.
steps: Return to each important article every couple of months to add new statistics, update wording, and reference recent case studies or product changes.
Add a clearly visible last-updated date to every article so AI and Google bots can see freshness without re-reading the whole page.

The presenter claims that even updating only the last-updated date — without changing content — can boost rankings; treat this as the presenter's assertion, and note it will not help if the underlying content is outdated or false.
Recognize that freshness is a ranking factor across search engines, not just AI, so the same maintenance serves traditional SEO.
Prioritize top-performing pages and high-commercial-intent content (category pages, comparison pages, top buying guides) when time is limited.
Avoid deceptive re-dating of unchanged content; the presenter describes this tactic as something to do 'really slightly so your competitors don't notice', which is an admission of manipulation.
caveats: The date-only freshness trick is grey-hat and the presenter frames it as something competitors should not notice; it carries reputational risk and no guarantee of lasting effect.
Real content updates are the durable version of this tactic.

cards.title: Fix NAP consistency and directory listings to stop AI misdescribing your store
cards.summary: Inconsistent name, address, phone and inconsistent descriptions across directories cause AI engines to produce wrong information about your business.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up brand presence for a store with physical locations, local service areas or notable B2B distribution, so AI shops describe it accurately.
steps: Complete your Google Business Profile with full, accurate details including what you sell, your USPs and how long you have operated.
Create and claim listings in business directories relevant to your category (the presenter names Yelp, Trustpilot, Crunchbase, and industry platforms) and on review platforms.

Ensure your business name, address and phone number are character-for-character consistent everywhere, since inconsistency causes AI to produce wrong information and reduces the chance of recommendation.
Encourage customers to leave reviews on the most relevant platforms, and keep review responses current.
Keep descriptions aligned with the checklist of what AI says it looks for when recommending your type of product (see the 'ask AI what it looks for' card below).
Re-audit listings when you rebrand, move, or add locations, because stale entries will keep feeding AI outdated facts.
caveats: The presenter lists directory platforms generically; which ones matter depends on your category and country.
Paid review-incentive programs must comply with platform rules — Google prohibits incentivized reviews, so check current policies before offering rewards.

cards.title: Get into 'best of' listicles and roundup articles that AI cites
cards.summary: AI engines frequently draw recommendations from '10 best X' listicles, so securing placement there directly increases the chance your store gets recommended.
cards.use_when: Acquiring recommendations in AI answers for a category where buyer queries surface best-of roundups (e.g. 'best [category] for [use case]').
steps: Search your key category term (e.g. 'best self storage software') in AI Overviews and AI mode and note which sources are used; the presenter's example showed listicles dominating the sources.
Click through to the listicle and identify the people who maintain it; install the Hunter Chrome extension to pull contact details of people at that site.
Reach out via email and LinkedIn with a credible, specific case for why your business belongs on the list — ideally near the top.
Expect that some listings require payment; the presenter says paying for placement can sharply increase AI visibility because listicles are a primary AI source.
Build a simple spreadsheet tracking every site you want to be featured on and work through it step by step rather than ad hoc.
Consider hiring a YouTube creator to produce a best-list video for your industry; video transcripts also get cited by AI engines.
caveats: The presenter states paid placements are sometimes necessary and calls it worth it; disclose paid placements where required and weigh the ethics and platform norms of your industry.
Getting listed does not guarantee a top recommendation, and paying does not override relevance.

cards.title: Ask AI what it looks for when recommending your product, then align every listing
cards.summary: Prompt AI engines for the criteria they use to recommend your category, then retrofit your website and directory descriptions to match those criteria.
cards.use_when: Setting the target for what your store's descriptions, PDPs and directory listings should contain in order to be recommended in AI answers.
steps: Open an AI engine (the presenter uses Gemini) and ask directly: 'What do you look for when recommending [your product or service category]?'
Capture the checklist of key pillars the AI names — these are the criteria it applies when choosing what to recommend.
Compare the checklist against your website copy and every place your business is listed; anywhere a criterion is missing, add it explicitly.

Example from the source: if you are the best website designer in New York, your descriptions must actually state that you are based in New York, work with New York businesses, and hold relevant local accreditations, or AI will not tie you to New York.
Repeat the prompt across multiple AI engines and merge the criteria into one master checklist.

Then ask AI: 'Search the internet and tell me what you know about my business', review the cited sources, and update each source's description (or contact the site owner) so it contains the checklist items.
caveats: AI-generated criteria are the model's stated reasoning, which may vary by engine, prompt wording and time; treat it as a research input, not a definitive algorithm.
If you cannot edit a source directly, you must persuade the site owner — an outreach task with uncertain success.

cards.title: Run an AI brand audit to find and correct the sources AI reads about you
cards.summary: Asking AI to search the internet and report what it knows about your brand reveals the exact sources shaping its view so you can fix them.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why AI engines describe an ecommerce store incorrectly, omit key categories, or recommend competitors instead.
steps: Prompt the AI: 'Search the internet and tell me what you know about [brand]' and read the answer as if you were a prospective buyer.
Open the cited sources listed under the answer — these are the pages the AI used to form its understanding of your business.

For each source you control, edit the description to include the criteria AI says it looks for; for sources you do not control, use contact-finding tools (e.g. Hunter) to reach the site owner and request a correction or an updated description.
Run the same prompt for each main competitor ('Search the internet and tell me what you know about competitor A/B/C/D') to see which sources drive their recommendations.
Aim to win mentions, or better, placement in listicles, on those same competitor-driving sources to capture recommendation share.
Repeat the audit periodically, since AI answers and their sources change over time.
caveats: Cited sources can vary run to run and across engines; treat the list as a starting point rather than a fixed map.
Editing third-party sources depends on cooperation or payment.

cards.title: Earn third-party mentions, podcasts and video to build AI trust
cards.summary: AI has no personal experience, so it looks for consensus; mentions in trusted publications, podcasts and video transcripts supply that consensus for your brand.
cards.use_when: Building authority signals for an ecommerce brand in a competitive category where reviews and editorial coverage influence AI recommendations.
steps: Secure mentions in at least three industry publications via guest posts, interviews or PR, prioritizing outlets AI cites in your category.

Approach industry accreditation bodies and associations — many allow sponsorship, contributed articles or partner listings; the presenter says paying may be necessary if you are serious about visibility.
Pitch industry podcasts, because transcripts are frequently indexed and cited by AI engines.
Work with influencers to post YouTube videos about the brand; the presenter's example video ranked on page one of Google and its transcript was also used as an AI source.
Structure any long-form external content (LinkedIn articles included) the same way as site content: value in the first 2-4 sentences, a TL;DR, and tables and bullets for easy extraction.
Track target publications and appearances in a spreadsheet so mention-building is systematic rather than opportunistic.
caveats: The presenter's claim that a video 'works like rocket fuel' is anecdotal; treat influencer/video coverage as one contributing signal.
Paid placements and sponsorships should be disclosed where required.

cards.title: Generate reviews with specific outcome language to feed AI consensus
cards.summary: Because AI has no first-hand experience, it leans on customer reviews — especially ones that state concrete results — to decide whether to recommend you.
cards.use_when: Designing a review-generation process for an ecommerce or high-ticket store to strengthen AI and traditional recommendation signals.
steps: Procure Google review cards with a QR code and NFC tag so staff can ask customers for a review immediately after a completed job or order.
Set up review requests for the platforms relevant to your category (the presenter names G2, Capterra, Trustpilot alongside Google).
Consider incentivizing staff $10-$20 per review to drive volume; the presenter estimates this may cost thousands per year but says the ROI is strong for high-ticket products.

Encourage reviewers to describe the specific outcomes they got — results with numbers — rather than generic praise; the presenter says specific example-based reviews make AI more likely to recommend you.
Steer review requests toward the platforms that AI actually cites for your category, and confirm current platform policies on incentivized reviews before running rewards.
Monitor new reviews and respond, since review content is part of the sentiment AI reads.
caveats: Paid or incentivized reviews violate the policies of several major platforms (including Google) and can lead to removal or penalties; check each platform's current rules.
The presenter's ROI argument assumes a high-ticket product; low-ticket stores should model the cost before scaling review incentives.

cards.title: Engage Reddit communities with F5Bot monitoring to earn long-term AI citations
cards.summary: Reddit is one of the most-cited sources in AI answers, and cited posts are typically over a year old, so consistent value-first participation compounds.
cards.use_when: Building durable category presence and word-of-mouth for a store where buyers discuss products in Reddit threads and forums.
steps: Identify five to ten subreddits most relevant to your product category.
Participate by providing free value in existing threads first, building account karma before ever mentioning your brand, so you reduce the risk of being banned when you do.
Set up F5Bot alerts for your key category keywords so you get notified whenever they are mentioned on Reddit and can respond while the thread is active.
When relevant, recommend your product naturally within a genuinely helpful answer rather than dropping a link cold.
Expect a long runway: the presenter says the average Reddit post cited by AI is over a year old, so this is a one-to-two-year compounding play, not a quick win.
The presenter reports brands applying this Reddit engagement approach have multiplied visibility several-fold — treat this as an anecdotal case result, not a promise.
caveats: Reddit communities penalize overt promotion; value-first participation is essential and results are slow.
The stated 4-5x visibility uplift is the presenter's claim about unnamed brands and is not independently verifiable.

cards.title: Publish long-form LinkedIn articles structured for AI extraction
cards.summary: Long-form LinkedIn articles get indexed by Google and can therefore become AI-cited sources, unlike short posts.
cards.use_when: Extending an ecommerce brand's content footprint onto LinkedIn to create additional citable sources about your products and expertise.
steps: Write long-form LinkedIn articles rather than short posts; the presenter notes long-form articles are indexed by Google, which makes them eligible as AI sources.
Structure them like your web content: deliver value in the first two to four sentences, include a TL;DR.
Add tables and bullet points so AI engines can easily extract key information to reuse in recommendations.
Cover core topics in your category and ideally include a natural recommendation of your product or service within the value.
Keep article facts consistent with your website and directory descriptions to reinforce rather than confuse AI's understanding.
Publish on a schedule; each article adds another potential citation surface.
caveats: LinkedIn indexing and discoverability of articles varies over time; verify current behavior rather than assuming permanent indexing.
Attribution of LinkedIn content to AI answers is not directly measurable in most setups.

cards.title: Use YouTube and video transcripts as a brand and AI citation channel
cards.summary: Video transcripts are indexed and cited by AI engines, so publishing videos about your products adds a durable discoverable source.
cards.use_when: Planning a video/content channel extension for an ecommerce brand to increase AI and Google discoverability.
steps: Create a YouTube channel and an introductory video about your business, even at modest production value; the presenter says this associates the channel with your brand and gives AI a transcript to read.
Pick a specific search term your target customers use across Google, YouTube and AI search engines.
Place that keyword or term in the video title, description, YouTube video filename and thumbnail filename, and say it in the first and last 10 seconds of the video.
Prioritize information value over production quality; the presenter emphasizes value to the target customer.
Produce a companion blog post for every video, and a video for every blog post, to multiply the footprint of each idea.
Link the YouTube channel from your website and include it in schema markup alongside your social profiles.
caveats: The presenter's claim of occupying multiple page-one spots in ChatGPT ads is a personal case, not a guaranteed outcome.
Keyword-in-filename and first/last-10-seconds tactics are the presenter's heuristics; platform ranking behavior changes over time.

cards.title: Use parasite SEO and self-published listicles on trusted platforms (grey hat)
cards.summary: Publishing your own 'best of' listicles on high-authority platforms can shift what LLMs say because small numbers of documents influence model answers.
cards.use_when: Aggressive AI-visibility campaigns for a store that accepts grey-hat tactics and wants to displace competitors in recommendation-style queries.
steps: Understand the cited premise: studies reportedly found as few as 10 documents can influence LLM outputs of any size, meaning a small set of consistent sources can change what AI says about your category.
Produce your own listicles that place your brand at the top and, in the aggressive version, omit competitors entirely.
Publish these listicles on already-trusted platforms — Medium, Substack, LinkedIn, Quora and any owned sites — since AI engines already weight these domains.
Publish five to ten such articles to reach the apparent influence threshold the presenter describes.
Then also target sources that currently drive competitors' recommendations: identify them via AI brand audits and try to place content there that favors you.
The presenter explicitly describes this as source poisoning and acknowledges some businesses may consider it unethical.
caveats: This is explicitly grey-hat/spam-adjacent; it risks platform penalties, reputational damage and erosion of consumer trust if discovered.
LLM source influence is not a stable, controllable mechanism — behavior changes as models and grounding sources are updated.

cards.title: Publish industry-report-style press releases to capture AI trust
cards.summary: Framing a listicle as a data-backed industry report and distributing it via a press wire is presented as one of the highest-ROI AI visibility moves.
cards.use_when: A category-level push to become the cited authority in AI answers, especially for a store or brand with data it can package as research.
steps: Title the release as an industry report, e.g. '[Niche] Industry Report: Top Leaders Ranked', rather than a plain 'Top 10' article.
Position the content as research findings you conducted and are releasing, which the presenter says AI engines trust more than self-serving listicles.
Include, where you have it, original data — AI engines look for unique data to cite and trust reports more than promotional posts.
Distribute the release via a press wire such as Newswire; the presenter says submissions cost a few hundred dollars and calls it likely the highest-ROI activity.
Consider including your own brand at the top of the rankings, and be aware the presenter treats that as the intent behind the format.
Repeat across categories or quarters to build a body of citable reports.
caveats: The presenter's claim that these reports are cited and trusted more than articles is based on personal tests with clients and community members — an anecdotal claim, not a controlled benchmark.
Self-serving industry reports can damage credibility if the underlying 'research' is not real; disclose methodology or expect skepticism.

cards.title: Execute a one-week AI visibility quick-win sequence
cards.summary: A prioritized starter list of free and low-cost actions to materially improve AI visibility within a week.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce operator starting AI visibility work and needing an ordered, immediately actionable checklist.
steps: Check robots.txt with a free AI bot access checker; register the site in Bing Webmaster Tools and Google Search Console and submit the sitemap.
Hire a YouTube creator to produce a best-providers list video for your industry and publish it on YouTube.
Add Organization schema linking to LinkedIn, Crunchbase and other reputable mentions of your brand, including social profiles.
Rewrite your business descriptions across all directories and review platforms using the checklist generated from asking AI what it looks for when recommending your offering.
Update your top three blog posts to add a TL;DR at the top and an FAQ section at the bottom.
Ask AI what it knows about you and correct the sources it cites; create new citations and review-platform entries and refresh existing ones.

Publish one long-form LinkedIn article on a core category topic that recommends your product, and start securing placement in 'best X' articles by finding AI-cited sources and outreaching via Hunter and LinkedIn.
caveats: These are the presenter's prioritization, not a validated sequence with measured effect sizes; treat the week as a starting sprint and re-measure.
Some steps (YouTube creation, paid placements) may cost money despite the 'free' framing in the video intro.
